title: From virtual to physical addresses
objectives: Split a virtual address into a page number and an offset
Use a page table to find the physical frame
Explain which part of the address stays unchanged

blocks.text: A program sees one continuous address space. Physical memory does not have to be continuous. Paging connects the two.
Virtual memory is divided into fixed-size pages. Physical memory is divided into frames of the same size. A page table maps each virtual page to a physical frame.
For a page size of 4 KiB (4,096 bytes), the lower 12 bits of an address identify a byte within the page. The remaining bits identify the virtual page number.

data.caption: The frame changes. The byte offset is preserved.

blocks.text: Take the virtual address 13,192. Divide by the page size to find the page number, and use the remainder as the offset. Here 13,192 = 3 × 4,096 + 904, so the page number is 3 and the offset is 904.

blocks.label: Pseudocode: address translation
blocks.text:
page_size = 4096
page = 13192 // page_size    # 3
offset = 13192 % page_size  # 904
frame = page_table[page]    # 5
physical = frame * page_size + offset
# 5 * 4096 + 904 = 21384
The result is 21,384, not 13,192. Only the page number is translated. The offset stays 904.

blocks.title: Keep the units straight
blocks.text: A page number is an index, not a byte address. Multiply the frame number by the page size before adding the offset.

blocks.question: With a 4 KiB page size and page_table[3] = 5, which physical address corresponds to virtual address 13,192?
blocks.explanation: 13,192 = 3 × 4,096 + 904, so the page number is 3 and the offset is 904. Frame 5 starts at 5 × 4,096 = 20,480, and adding the offset gives 21,384. The value 20,480 forgets the offset.
